newsitem.title: USA: Westinghouse seen splitting into two - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Westinghouse seen splitting into two - analysts.

text.p: Westinghouse Electric Corp., once a pillar of industrial America, appears set to split into two -- a manufacturing company and a company centred on its more promising media business, Wall Street analysts said Tuesday.
For the past year, Pittsburgh-based Westinghouse has been shedding industrial assets and aggressively building its portfolio of media properties.

After acquiring CBS Inc. for $5.4 billion a year ago, Westinghouse in short order agreed to sell its Knoll furniture unit for $565 million and its defence electronics business to Northrop Grumman Corp. for $3.6 billion.

Last summer it agreed to buy Infinity Broadcasting, the nation's second-largest radio broadcaster, in a deal worth $3.9 billion and Telenoticias, the world's leading Spanish language news channel. Terms in the Telenoticias deal were not disclosed.
Ever since it said in June that it was weighing such a move, investors have expected Westinghouse to move to split the media business from the rest of its industrial operations.

Westinghouse declined to comment on the speculation Tuesday but said it would hold a news conference Wednesday afternoon. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the company's board was meeting to approve a plan to split the businesses that could be unveiled as early as Wednesday.
Analysts said Westinghouse would probably name the media company Westinghouse/CBS and locate its headquarters in New York. The industrial operations will likely remain based in Pittsburgh, they said.
"But what they're going to call that company is anybody's guess," said Nick Heymann at NatWest Heymann.
Sources said Westinghouse would also sell its headquarters building in downtown Pittsburgh and move employees there to locations in the suburbs.
Commercial real estate sources in Pittsburgh said recently that Westinghouse has been quietly seeking a buyer for the building. The company has repeatedly declined to comment.
"I understand they've been shopping that building around," said Rich Beynon at Beynon & Co., a commercial real estate firm.
"I can guarantee you they're going to sell that building. It's just a question of when," another real estate official said.

Analysts said they could not confirm when an announcement might come, but lauded the expected move since it would unlock the value of Westinghouse's media businesses, now masked by its older, less-profitable industrial businesses.
"Splitting the company into separate entities will get people focused on the part of the company they're most interested in," said Kent Newcomb at A.G. Edwards. "That clearly should be a positive.
With the exception of Thermo King, a refrigerated transportation business, Westinghouse's industrial operations have been a drag on earnings, analysts said.
Conversely, the media business has thrived. The radio operations posted sales gains in the third quarter that outpaced rivals, and CBS has boosted the network's ratings since its acquisition.

Westinghouse is expected to close its purchase of radio giant Infinity Broadcasting by year-end. The Justice Department approved the merger Tuesday, but with the stipulation that the companies agree to sell radio stations in Boston and Philadelphia.
Westinghouse stock added 62.5 cents to close at $20.625 on the New York Stock Exchange after hitting a 52-week high of $21.125.
